title: Sikh studies
hook: universities around the world teach Sikh history and scripture

segments.voice: Yesterday, phulkari: silk flowers on hand-spun cotton, given at weddings. Your line was stitched flowers. Whom did you thank for something made slowly? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

What happens when a scripture becomes a subject on a syllabus? On a gray afternoon in a lecture hall far from Punjab, a professor puts a page of Gurmukhi on the screen, and a room of students, some in turbans, some meeting the Gurus for the first time this term, lean in to work out a single line. Down the corridor, a graduate student is reading old manuscripts for a thesis. Universities far from Punjab, as well as in it, teach Sikh history and scripture. Today's word is that field.
screen: `A PAGE OF GURMUKHI ON THE SCREEN.` → `STUDENTS OF EVERY BACKGROUND.` → `A SHELF THAT KEEPS GROWING.`

segments.voice: First, what Sikh studies is. It's the academic study of the Sikh tradition: its scripture and languages, its history, its music and art, its life in Punjab and in every place Sikhs have settled. Students learn Gurmukhi, read the Guru Granth Sahib closely, and ask how the panth grew. Second, an early bridge. A British official named Max Arthur Macauliffe worked beside Sikh scholars, among them Bhai Kahn Singh of Nabha, to put the Gurus' hymns and lives into English, in a work called The Sikh Religion. He leaned on Sikh learning at every step. This path still quotes his English in places. Third, an honest tension. Some Sikhs welcome study of their tradition, and some communities have helped fund chairs and programs. At times, though, a historian's reading of a manuscript or a story has unsettled Sikhs who hold a different understanding, and there have been real arguments. Sikh scholars work inside the universities too, holding faith and research together. Both trust and caution are part of the story. Fourth, what Guru Nanak said about reading. In the Asa di Var he pictures someone reading cartloads of books, reading for months and years, all through life. And then, in paraphrase: only one thing is of account; the rest is the chatter of ego. Some readers take that one thing as the Name. Study can serve it, or it can get in the way. And this week has walked through the panth's arts: kavishri, katha, the ragas, painting, buildings, phulkari, and now the study of it all. Studied everywhere.
screen: `THE ACADEMIC STUDY OF THE PANTH.` · `MACAULIFFE AND BHAI KAHN SINGH.` · `TRUST, AND CAUTION.` · `CARTLOADS OF BOOKS, ONE THING.` · then, large: `STUDIED EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one scholarly article. Settle, and breathe. For now, just choose: a question about the Sikh tradition you'd genuinely like answered. Hold it. Where did the Gurmukhi script come from? How was the Granth put together? What do the ragas mean? After the bell, look for one careful article on it, from a university or a scholarly journal, and read it slowly. And keep Guru Nanak's line beside you while you read: one thing is of account. The bell holds the time.
Sikh studies. The academic study of the Sikh tradition, its scripture, history and arts, taught in universities far from Punjab as well as in it. Today's word.
Your line: studied everywhere. Today, learn one fact about a tradition that isn't yours from a careful source, and notice what changes when you know it. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.
